section_summary: This section consists chiefly of petitions and letters from Methodist clergy, congregations, conference participants, and private citizens urging the Roosevelt administration to halt American exports of arms, aircraft, fuel, scrap iron, credit, and other war-sustaining supplies to Japan. State Department replies repeatedly explain that invoking the Neutrality Act would embargo both China and Japan, that the law did not authorize a unilateral or comprehensive embargo, and that the President judged invocation contrary to American interests; several replies cite licensed arms exports of roughly $13.97 million to China and $10.38 million to Japan. The section concludes with a forty-one-page resolution and signature list from the Old Salem Epworth League Institute in Illinois calling for reduced American armament spending and an end to munitions shipments to the Orient.

subfiles.title: Letter from Senior Bishop Edwin Holt Hughes urging an end to war-sustaining trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Hughes asks the President to stop American traffic with Japan that contributes to the destruction of Chinese lives and property.
subfiles.summary: Senior Methodist bishop Edwin Hughes urges Roosevelt to end American commerce aiding Japan's war, saying a large public majority would support it.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Edwin Holt Hughes on the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the administration has not invoked the Neutrality Act or imposed a unilateral embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Moore says a war finding would bar arms to both sides, no Japan-only or non-arms authority exists; licensed arms since July 1, 1937: about $13.97 million to China, $10.38 million to Japan.

subfiles.title: Herbert Welch to Cordell Hull concerning exports of war materials to Japan
subfiles.about: Welch asks whether existing legislation can be used to stop the shipment of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bishop Welch supports Hull but says Americans are ashamed their resources are used against China, and asks whether action is possible without new legislation.

subfiles.title: Herbert Welch to President Roosevelt requesting an embargo on Japan
subfiles.about: Welch urges Roosevelt to place an embargo on Japanese war supplies if existing law permits it.
subfiles.summary: Welch tells Roosevelt Americans feel shame over supplying Japan's war needs and believes opinion would favor a Japan-specific embargo if legal.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Herbert Welch
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department responds jointly to Welch's letters to Hull and Roosevelt concerning an embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reply to Welch: the Neutrality Act needs a presidential war finding and would stop arms to China too; Roosevelt judged invocation against American interests; license values cited.

subfiles.title: W. I. Farmer transmits the Decatur, Tennessee, mass-meeting resolution
subfiles.about: Farmer reports a unanimous resolution asking the President and Congress to prevent American resources from aiding Japan's aggression.
subfiles.summary: W. I. Farmer reports 134 attended a Decatur, Tennessee mass meeting whose resolution condemns Japan's invasion and asks federal measures against direct or indirect aid.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to W. I. Farmer
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the Decatur resolution and gives the standard legal explanation for not embargoing Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department says the resolution will receive appropriate consideration. Yost explains that the Neutrality Act would apply equally to China and Japan and that no authority existed to prohibit other commodities or Japan alone. He adds that Roosevelt judged invocation contrary to national interests and supplies comparative arms-license totals.

subfiles.title: F. A. Hinman transmits Lakeside conference resolutions
subfiles.about: Hinman forwards resolutions adopted by a religious conference as evidence of growing Christian opposition to supplying Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hinman sends Lakeside conference resolutions as evidence of growing Christian sentiment; handwriting degraded.

subfiles.title: Resolution of the Bible Conference of Religion and Life at Lakeside, Ohio
subfiles.from: Ministers and laymen attending the Bible Conference of Religion and Life
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull and Ohio's congressional delegation
subfiles.about: Conference participants call for withholding war materials and credit from Japan while opposing military intervention.
subfiles.summary: Lakeside Bible Conference resolution condemns Japan's undeclared war and civilian bombing, rejects military intervention but urges withdrawing war materials and credit, and sympathizes with both peoples.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to F. A. Hinman
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost answers the Lakeside resolution with the Department's Neutrality Act position.
subfiles.summary: Yost to Hinman: a war finding would embargo arms to both sides; law does not allow a Japan-only embargo or controls on other commodities; license figures.

subfiles.title: Elizabeth Chambers to Cordell Hull criticizing Far Eastern policy
subfiles.about: Chambers criticizes the administration for protesting Japanese conduct while permitting American business and war supplies to sustain Japan.
subfiles.summary: Chambers praises protests against attacks on civilians but doubts a policy leaving the Neutrality Act unused, criticizes oil and tobacco firms in China, and urges discouraging exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Elizabeth Chambers
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Chambers's criticism and explains its legal and policy position on exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost says a proclamation would bar exports to both sides and not cover commodities beyond arms; cites license totals and Hull's June 11 statement discouraging aircraft sales.

subfiles.title: John Arthur West conveys his church conference's appeal
subfiles.about: West reports a unanimous church vote urging action against war-sustaining trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: John West, for a Warren, Rhode Island Methodist quarterly conference, asks Hull to help end commerce making the US a partner in the Far Eastern conflict.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to John Arthur West
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost answers West's request for an embargo with the Department's interpretation of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that a presidential proclamation would stop arms exports to both belligerents, while the government lacked authority to single out Japan or prohibit other commodities. It states that Roosevelt judged invocation inconsistent with the country's broader interests. Export-license totals for China and Japan are again supplied.

subfiles.title: W. Kyle Cregger transmits a signed resolution on the Sino-Japanese War
subfiles.about: Cregger forwards a church resolution signed by adults and voting-age young people.
subfiles.summary: Cregger sends a signed resolution representing his church and community, presented to classes without active solicitation, and says the church prays for action.

subfiles.title: Signed Anderson Street Methodist Church resolution on the Sino-Japanese War
subfiles.from: Members of Anderson Street M. E. Church, South
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: The petition asks the government to prevent American material and financial resources from assisting Japan's aggression against China.
subfiles.summary: The repeated resolution declares that Japan invaded China and that American war materials and supplies were causing Chinese suffering and loss of life and property. It calls upon the President and Congress to prevent government or private resources from aiding Japan directly or indirectly. Seven pages carry handwritten signatures, many of which are badly degraded in the OCR.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to W. Kyle Cregger
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the signed petition and explains why the government has not invoked the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The Department promises careful consideration of the resolution. Yost says the law would prohibit arms shipments to both China and Japan after a presidential finding of war and could not support a unilateral Japanese embargo. He reiterates Roosevelt's national-interest judgment and gives the standard comparative figures for licensed arms exports.

subfiles.title: Donald H. Gibbs forwards the Old Salem Epworth League Institute resolution
subfiles.about: Gibbs submits a resolution signed by approximately seven hundred Methodist young people and ministers.
subfiles.summary: Gibbs forwards the Old Salem Epworth League resolution from Illinois youth leaders petitioning for changes on armaments and munitions exports to the Orient.

subfiles.title: Old Salem Epworth League Institute resolution and signature rolls
subfiles.from: Faculty and students of the Old Salem Epworth League Institute
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: Hundreds of Illinois Methodists urge reduced domestic armament spending and an end to shipments of gasoline, oil, scrap iron, aircraft, ammunition, and other munitions to the Orient.
subfiles.summary: The resolution deplores civilian and military deaths in China and acknowledges the American role in teaching Western warfare and supplying both China and Japan. It declares war an unsuitable means of settling international disputes and argues that American armament policy threatens world peace and domestic welfare. The petition requests reductions in American arms expenditures and a halt to exports of fuel, scrap iron, aircraft, ammunition, and related supplies to the Orient. The remaining pages consist of extensive name, city, and state columns, with many names duplicated or badly distorted by handwriting recognition and OCR.
